clue.text: Chased to derelict terminals

indicators.note: derelict means run-down and in disorder, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is pursued to abandoned railway or bus termini.
explanation.walkthrough: 'derelict' rearranges CHASED and TO together. 'terminals' looks like the stations of the surface, but here it means electrodes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathodes are electrodes, the negative terminals of a battery or electrolytic cell.

clue.text: Strike about to stop working

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for strike goes round the next word

parts.note: to cuff is to strike with the hand

explanation.surface: A labour leader says that a strike is about to halt the plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is a container signal and 'to' is a piece of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine or power supply that cuts off stops running suddenly.

clue.text: Like a wedding cake dieter cooked

indicators.note: cooked means altered or doctored, as when books are cooked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A slimmer bakes a wedding cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' fits the baking scene but rearranges DIETER.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional wedding cake is built in stacked layers, one above another.

clue.text: Flashy coupe at Silverstone initially goes faster

indicators.note: flashy means showy and wild, so the letters of the words after it are thrown about
initially tells us to take only the first letter of the racetrack name

explanation.surface: A showy sports car at the British Grand Prix circuit overtakes the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flashy' rearranges COUPE AT to OUTPACE, and 'initially' adds the S of Silverstone. Silverstone is a motor-racing circuit in England.
explanation.definitionFit: To outpace rivals is to move more quickly than them, leaving them behind.

clue.text: Poetry losing very old language

indicators.note: losing tells us a letter drops out of the word for poetry

parts.note: verse is poetry

explanation.surface: A verse form that has given up very ancient tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' takes the V (very) out of VERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic tongue of Scotland and Ireland.

clue.text: Give credit to monkey's curls

parts.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for credit in accounts
a monkey is a mischievous child, an imp; with the 's this gives the plural-looking IMPS

explanation.surface: An invitation to praise a monkey for its curly coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'monkey' means a little rascal, an imp, not the animal; 'Give' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimps are small tight waves or curls put into hair.

clue.text: Harvester being grim when you're late

definitions.meaning: someone or something that cuts and gathers a crop
the Grim one is Death, who comes when you are late in the sense of dead

explanation.surface: A farmhand looks gloomy when you turn up late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' means dead, not tardy: the Grim Reaper is Death personified.
explanation.definitionFit: A reaper cuts corn at harvest, and the Grim Reaper is Death with his scythe.

clue.text: Goo on loo perhaps is to spread quickly

parts.note: goo is soft gloop, mush
a loo is one example of a room in a house; perhaps marks the example

explanation.surface: Gloop on the lavatory spreads fast.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'too' is an OCR slip for 'loo'; 'on' is a link word placing goo first, and 'perhaps' marks an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To mushroom is to grow or expand rapidly, as fungi spring up overnight.

clue.text: Mum's more embarrassed being destroyer of sensitive material

parts.note: mum means silent, and SH is the call for silence; the 's is 'is'
embarrassed people go red, so more embarrassed is redder

explanation.surface: Mother is even more embarrassed at being the one who ruins delicate stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' means keeping quiet, not mother, giving SH.
explanation.definitionFit: A shredder cuts confidential papers into strips so they cannot be read.

clue.text: I restate profound theory

indicators.note: profound here suggests the words are turned over deeply and thoroughly, so the letters of I RESTATE are rearranged

explanation.surface: A thinker announces that they are repeating a deep theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'profound' looks like a description of the theory, but it signals that I RESTATE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written exposition setting out a systematic argument or doctrine.

clue.text: Ruler's motor with a lot of water in back

indicators.note: in tells us the turned piece goes inside the word for motor

parts.note: motor is an informal word for a car

indicators.note: back tells us the word for a lot of water is read from right to left

parts.note: a sea is a large body of water

explanation.surface: A ruler's car has a lot of water sloshing in its rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like the rear of the car, but it is the reversal signal, and 'in' is the container signal; 'with' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar was the title of the Roman emperors, so a supreme ruler.

clue.text: Ready to change long ago!

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters of the two words before it

explanation.surface: Someone declares themselves set for change after a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges READY TO. 'The year dot' is British slang for a very long time ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Since the year dot means since the beginning of time, a very distant past.

clue.text: Boxer George has no right to be the enemy

indicators.note: has no tells us a letter is missing from the boxer's surname

parts.note: George Foreman was a world heavyweight boxing champion

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer, lacking the right, is cast as the villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no' takes the R out of FOREMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Foeman is an archaic word for an opponent in war, an adversary.

clue.text: Judge made mistake and looked up

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a match
to err is to make a mistake, so erred means made a mistake

explanation.surface: A referee blundered and then checked the rule book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' is a sporting official here, and 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To have referred to a book or source is to have consulted it, as when checking a dictionary.

clue.text: Gasp for breath by girl's big cat

parts.note: to pant is to gasp for breath
her is the possessive for a girl

explanation.surface: A girl's huge cat is out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link word, and 'girl's' gives a possessive pronoun rather than a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A panther is a large wild feline, a leopard or puma.

clue.text: Doctors on doubles…

parts.note: RE means on or concerning, as in letter headings
doubles are twos of a kind, pairs

explanation.surface: Physicians working on doubles at tennis, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' is a verb here: it fixes things. The dots join this clue to the next as one surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To doctor a thing is to patch it up or mend it, so doctors means fixes.

clue.text: …sweat endless hooch

indicators.note: endless tells us the word for hooch loses one of its ends, here its first letter

parts.note: hooch is slang for alcoholic drink, booze

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: the players sweat out the cheap liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' removes just one end, the B at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweat seeps out of the skin, and to ooze is to seep out slowly.

clue.text: Enthusiast is the last to clap Thatcher?

indicators.note: the last to tells us to take the final letter of clap

parts.note: a thatcher who roofs with straw is a craftsman, an artisan; the question mark admits the example

explanation.surface: A supporter is the final one to applaud Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' suggests the prime minister, but it is a roofer, an example of a skilled tradesman. 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan is a strong supporter of a party or cause, a zealous follower.

clue.text: Where batsman is to expand

definitions.meaning: a batsman taking guard stands at the crease, the line marked in front of the stumps, so is in the crease

explanation.surface: Where a cricketer stands, getting bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the crease is the line where the batsman stands, so a batsman is 'in crease'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at the crease in cricket is being in it, and to increase is to grow or enlarge.

clue.text: Edible snails? Definitely not!

parts.note: snails are slow movers, so food made of them is the opposite of quick grub; read the other way, it is takeaway meals served in a hurry

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to eat escargots.
explanation.walkthrough: Snails are proverbially slow, so a meal of them would be the very opposite of quick, ready-made food.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgers and takeaways served at speed are the opposite of slow-moving snails.

clue.text: Johannesburg captivates her

indicators.note: captivates suggests the city name holds a shorter word captive within it

explanation.surface: A woman is charmed by Johannesburg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivates' shows the name sits inside JOHANNESBURG; 'her' stands for any woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name stands for a female person, referred to as her.

clue.text: Tomato squashed by new cushion

indicators.note: a squashed tomato is out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tomato gets flattened by someone sitting on a new cushion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squashed' rearranges TOMATO to OTTOMA, and 'by' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An ottoman is a low upholstered seat or footstool, a padded seat like a large cushion.

clue.text: What makes Sal's shoe?

parts.note: the name Sal is formed by S joined to AL, and that phrase, read as one word, is a kind of open footwear

explanation.surface: What makes Sally's footwear?
explanation.walkthrough: Spell out how SAL is built: S + AND + AL, and the joined phrase is the shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandal is an open shoe held on by straps.

clue.text: Heart of French fish extracted for toxin

indicators.note: heart of points to the middle letter of the French word
extracted tells us that middle letter is taken out

parts.note: poisson is the French word for fish

explanation.surface: A French chef removes the heart of a fish to make a poison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of' with 'extracted' takes out the middle letter of POISSON, the fourth of seven, an S.
explanation.definitionFit: A toxin is a poisonous substance produced by a living thing.

clue.text: A learner's to request a cold place

parts.note: L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
to ask is to request

explanation.surface: A learner driver has to ask for a freezing place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'learner' and 'to' are link words; L is the learner plate on British cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Alaska is the northernmost US state, known for its icy climate.

clue.text: Mad Hatter points to indicate danger

indicators.note: mad means crazed and out of order, so the letters of the next word are scrambled

parts.note: E and N are compass points, east and north

explanation.surface: Alice's Mad Hatter gestures menacingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like part of the character's name, but it rearranges HATTER; 'points' means compass points. 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To threaten is to give warning of harm, to signal that trouble is coming.

clue.text: Small ugly dwarf's to walk in a leisurely manner

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a troll in folklore is an ugly dwarf or giant

explanation.surface: A small, ugly creature ambles along.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'dwarf' is 'is', and 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroll is an unhurried walk, and to stroll is to amble.

clue.text: Fish with a bit at the end

parts.note: cod is a fish

explanation.surface: A fish that has a little piece at its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word; the definition is musical, not about fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A coda is the concluding passage of a musical piece.

clue.text: Quiet guy's drink

parts.note: SH is the call for quiet
Andy is a man's name, so any guy; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A shy man's tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guy' is any man, here named as ANDY.
explanation.definitionFit: A shandy is a drink of beer mixed with lemonade.

clue.text: Giant firm's defeat by America

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
a defeat is a loss
US stands for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A huge company is beaten by an American rival.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'firm' and 'by' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A colossus is a statue or person of enormous size, like the Colossus of Rhodes.

clue.text: Injection causes irritation

definitions.meaning: a jab or shot is given through a hypodermic

explanation.surface: A jab makes the skin sore.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypodermic sharp gives a jab, and to needle someone is to goad and annoy them.

clue.text: Girl put stripe on top of scarf

indicators.note: on top of tells us the stripe word goes before the girl's name

parts.note: a stripe is a band of colour
Anna is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl sews a stripe on top of her scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on top of' simply means placed before; 'put' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandanna is a large coloured handkerchief worn as a neckerchief or headscarf.
